questions.text: Fill in the option that checks which version of Python is installed in the DEVASC VM.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step a: python3 -V (capital V) prints the installed version — Python 3.8.2 in the DEVASC VM.

questions.text: Fill in the command that shows where the local Python environment lives.
questions.explanation: Part 2, Step b: which python3 shows the path of the python3 the shell runs — /usr/bin/python3.

questions.text: What does PIP stand for?
questions.explanation: Part 3 intro: “PIP stands for Pip Installs Packages” — a recursive acronym.

questions.text: Why is running pip3 install on the system-wide Python installation discouraged?
options: System-wide installs need an internet connection every time Python starts
It can introduce competing dependencies that you may not want for every Python project
pip3 only works inside a virtual environment
Packages installed system-wide are deleted when you log out
questions.explanation: Part 3 intro: installing on the system might introduce competing dependencies that you may or may not want for all Python projects. The best practice is a virtual environment per project, with only the packages that project needs.

questions.text: According to the lab, which are benefits of working inside a Python virtual environment? (Choose all that apply.)
options: You know exactly which packages are installed in a given setting
You can switch package dependencies easily by switching to another virtual environment
You avoid breaking things with competing versions of software
Packages install faster because the virtual environment skips downloading them
Python itself is upgraded to the newest version inside the environment
questions.explanation: Part 3 intro: in a virtual environment you know exactly which packages are installed, you can switch dependencies easily when switching to a new virtual environment, and you don't break things through competing versions. A venv doesn't skip downloads or upgrade Python — it uses the Python it was created with.

questions.text: Which Python 3 tool does the lab use to create a virtual environment?
questions.explanation: Part 3 intro: “use the venv tool in Python 3 and then activate the virtual environment.” venv ships with Python 3; the others are separate tools.

questions.text: Before creating the virtual environment, which directory does the lab move into?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1a: cd labs/devnet-src/python/, which changes the prompt to devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to create a Python 3 virtual environment named devfun.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b: python3 -m venv devfun. The -m switch tells Python to run the venv module.

questions.text: In python3 -m venv devfun, what does the -m switch do?
options: Tells Python to run the venv module
Marks the environment as the default for every project
Runs Python in minimal mode with no packages
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b: “The -m switch tells Python to run the venv module.”

questions.text: The virtual environment has to be named devfun for venv to work.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 1b: “The name is chosen by the programmer.” Later in the lab you make a second one called devnew.

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to activate the devfun virtual environment.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2a: source devfun/bin/activate runs the environment's activate script in the current shell.

questions.text: After activating the virtual environment, how can you tell which environment you're working in?
options: The prompt starts with the environment's name in parentheses, e.g. (devfun)
A message saying Environment activated is printed
The terminal title bar changes to venv
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2a: “The prompt changes to indicate the name of the environment you are currently working in” — (devfun) devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$. >>> is the Python interpreter's prompt, not a venv's.

questions.text: While devfun is active, pip3 install only installs packages into the active virtual environment.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2a: once activated, “when you use the pip3 install command from here, the system will only install packages for the active virtual environment.”

questions.text: Right after activating the brand-new devfun environment, what does pip3 freeze show in the lab?
options: Every package installed system-wide, like ansible and xmltodict
Nothing — no additional packages are installed yet
An error, because freeze needs a file name
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2b: pip3 freeze verifies there are no additional Python packages in devfun — the prompt just comes back with no output. A fresh venv doesn't see the system's packages.

questions.text: Fill in the blank to install the requests package into the devfun environment.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2c: pip3 install requests.

questions.text: Installing requests also pulled in its dependencies. Which packages did pip3 install along with it? (Choose all that apply.)
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2c output: “Installing collected packages: urllib3, idna, certifi, chardet, requests.” ansible and xmltodict only show up in the system environment's freeze in Step 3.

questions.text: What format does pip3 freeze list each installed package in?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2d: each line is package==version. Part 4 explains that this exact format is what lets the list be reused as a requirements file.

questions.text: Fill in the command that leaves the virtual environment and goes back to the system.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 2e: deactivate. The (devfun) prefix disappears from the prompt.

questions.text: Fill in the blank to list the packages installed in the system environment.
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: python3 -m pip freeze, run after deactivating, lists the system-wide packages.

questions.text: Why does python3 -m pip freeze use pip rather than pip3?
options: Python 3 is already invoked by the command, so its module is just pip
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a note: “Because Python 3 is invoked with the following command, you only use pip instead of pip3.” -m pip runs the pip module of whichever Python you called.

questions.text: Which of these appears in the system environment's python3 -m pip freeze output, but not in devfun's?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3a: the system list starts with ansible==2.9.4, apache-libcloud==2.8.0, appdirs==1.4.3… The other three were installed into devfun as dependencies of requests.

questions.text: Fill in the symbol that sends the freeze output to grep to find the requests version.
questions.code: devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$ python3 -m pip freeze ___ grep requests
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3b: pipe (|) the output to grep to quickly find a package's version.

questions.text: python3 -m pip freeze | grep requests prints five lines, not one. Why?
options: grep prints every line that contains requests anywhere, including other packages whose names start with it
Five different versions of requests are installed at the same time
pip freeze repeats a package once per dependency
grep always prints the matching line plus the next four
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3b: grep requests matches any line containing the text, so requests-kerberos, requests-ntlm, requests-toolbelt and requests-unixsocket show up too. Only requests==2.22.0 is the requests package itself (checked by running the same grep on those five lines).

questions.text: What version of requests is installed in the system environment?
questions.explanation: Part 3, Step 3b: requests==2.22.0. devfun got requests-2.23.0 in Step 2c, and the two don't interfere — that's the point of a virtual environment. 0.12.0 is requests-kerberos.

questions.text: Why is the output of pip3 freeze in a specific format?
options: So other people working on the same project can recreate the same environment from it
So Python can import it as a module
So the packages can be uninstalled in one command
questions.explanation: Part 4 intro: “You can use all the dependencies listed so that other people who want to work on the same project as you can get the same environment as yours.”

questions.text: Fill in the symbol that saves the freeze output to a file called requirements.txt.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step b: pip3 freeze > requirements.txt. The > redirects the command's output into the file instead of the screen.

questions.text: Which environment must be active when you run pip3 freeze > requirements.txt to capture devfun's packages?
options: devfun — so the freeze lists its packages
None — deactivate first so the system packages are included
It doesn't matter; pip3 freeze always lists every environment
questions.explanation: Part 4, Steps a–b: re-activate devfun with source devfun/bin/activate, then freeze. Without it, you'd capture the system's packages instead.

questions.text: After deactivating devfun, where does ls show requirements.txt?
options: Nowhere — the file is deleted on deactivate
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step c: ls in the python directory lists requirements.txt next to devfun, devices.txt, hello-world.py and the other files. The redirect writes to the current directory; deactivating doesn't touch it. (The lab's listing also shows devnew, which isn't created until the next step.)

questions.text: Fill in the blanks to create and then activate a new virtual environment called devnew.
questions.code:
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$ python3 -m venv ___
devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$ ___ devnew/bin/activate
(devnew) devasc@labvm:~/labs/devnet-src/python$
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step d: python3 -m venv devnew, then source devnew/bin/activate. Same two steps as for devfun, just a different name.

questions.text: Fill in the option that installs every package listed in requirements.txt.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step e: pip3 install -r requirements.txt installs the same packages devfun has. -r means “read requirements from this file”.

questions.text: When installing from requirements.txt into devnew, pip printed Using cached certifi-2020.4.5.1-…whl instead of Downloading. Why?
options: Those same package files were already downloaded for devfun, so pip reused them from its cache
The packages were copied from the system environment
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step e output: the exact same versions were downloaded in Part 3, Step 2c, and pip keeps downloaded wheels in a cache. Each venv still gets its own installed copy — devnew and devfun don't share packages.

questions.text: During pip3 install -r requirements.txt in devnew, which requirement was reported as already satisfied instead of being collected?
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step e: “Requirement already satisfied: pkg-resources==0.0.0 in ./devnew/lib/python3.8/site-packages (from -r requirements.txt (line 4))”. Ubuntu's Python puts this placeholder in every new venv, so devnew already had it, and pip3 freeze lists it (Step f). It being on line 4 of requirements.txt means devfun's freeze had it too.
questions.warning: Upon double checking, devfun's pip3 freeze in Part 3 would also list pkg-resources==0.0.0 — the lab's screenshots there leave it out, but requirements.txt (made from that freeze) has it on line 4.

questions.text: After pip3 install -r requirements.txt, running pip3 freeze in devnew shows the same packages and versions as devfun.
questions.explanation: Part 4, Step f: devnew lists certifi==2020.4.5.1, chardet==3.0.4, idna==2.9, pkg-resources==0.0.0, requests==2.23.0 and urllib3==1.25.9 — exactly what was in requirements.txt. That's how the environment is shared.

questions.text: Match each command to what it does in the lab.
allChoices: Creates a virtual environment named devfun
Lists the packages installed in the active environment
Saves the package list to a file
Installs every package listed in a file

pairs.match: Creates a virtual environment named devfun
Lists the packages installed in the active environment
Saves the package list to a file
Installs every package listed in a file

questions.explanation: Parts 3 and 4: create with python3 -m venv, activate with source …/bin/activate, list with pip3 freeze, leave with deactivate, save with pip3 freeze > requirements.txt, and rebuild elsewhere with pip3 install -r requirements.txt.
